paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can perform well without acquiring several distinct ways to act. This paper links that difficulty to the commonly used Gaussian policy representation and introduces Di-SkilL, a method that represents skills through a mixture of experts. Each expert describes a contextual motion primitive, connecting a particular skill to the circumstances in which it operates.

Di-SkilL jointly optimizes each expert and the distribution of contexts it encounters. A maximum entropy objective encourages diverse skills even in similar contexts. The separate context distributions also create automatic curricula: each expert can concentrate on the part of the context space where it performs best. Skill specialization and the selection of learning situations are therefore developed together.

The method uses energy-based models to represent context distributions with abrupt changes or multiple modes, without prior knowledge of the environment’s context probability space. The authors show how to train these distributions using a standard policy gradient objective. Results on challenging robot simulation tasks demonstrate that Di-SkilL can acquire skills that are both varied and effective.
icml-2024-acquiring-diverse-skills-using.tldr: Di-SkilL combines expert policies with automatic curricula to learn diverse, effective skills in robot simulations.

paragraphs: An AI system can affect both what a user receives and what that user comes to want. This paper studies the alignment problems that arise when preferences change, including changes caused by interaction with the AI itself. It introduces Dynamic Reward Markov Decision Processes to make those changes and the system’s influence explicit.

The analysis shows that treating preferences as fixed may give existing alignment techniques unintended incentives. A system can implicitly be rewarded for changing users’ preferences in ways they would not truly want. The authors examine how the length of an agent’s optimization horizon may partially reduce undesirable influence, offering a shared perspective on this possible mitigation.

They also formalize and compare eight notions of alignment that incorporate changing preferences from the start. Each examined notion tends toward either undesirable influence or excessive risk aversion. This comparison suggests that a straightforward solution may be unavailable; it does not establish that every possible solution must fail. The contribution is a framework for reasoning explicitly about the tension between useful capabilities and influence over human preferences.
icml-2024-ai-alignment-with-changing-and.tldr: Modeling changing preferences reveals unwanted influence incentives and difficult tradeoffs in eight proposed notions of AI alignment.

paragraphs: Differential privacy provides an upper bound on how much information an algorithm could reveal, while an empirical audit establishes a lower bound on leakage demonstrated in practice. This paper brings auditing to private prediction, where privacy protection operates when a model answers queries. That extends the focus beyond existing audits of private training algorithms.

The framework constructs adversaries with different abilities to poison data and control prediction queries. It studies four private prediction methods: PATE, CaPC, PromptPATE, and Private-kNN. The authors also introduce techniques for measuring empirical leakage in terms of Rényi differential privacy, connecting their experiments to a formal privacy accounting framework.

The experiments indicate that the privacy analysis of private prediction can be improved. They also find substantially greater leakage in algorithms that are easier to poison, and significantly less leakage when adversaries lack query control. Together, these results show why an audit’s adversary capabilities matter: the practical leakage demonstrated by an attack depends on both the prediction mechanism and the access available to the attacker.
icml-2024-auditing-private-prediction-b4.tldr: A framework for auditing private prediction shows how poisoning and query control affect experimentally demonstrated privacy leakage.

paragraphs: Selecting a representative panel raises a question beyond who gets a seat: how well will its decisions reflect the population’s preferences? This paper examines sortition panels using metric distortion, a concept from computational social choice. The analysis places agents and preferences in a metric space and measures how closely a panel’s decision approaches the population’s ideal decision.

The first result concerns uniform selection. The authors show that a panel containing only logarithmically many agents in the number of alternatives can achieve almost optimal distortion. This is a statement about decision quality within the metric model. It provides a positive answer to whether relatively small panels can make decisions that align well with the larger population.

The paper also analyzes Fair Greedy Capture, an existing selection algorithm. It matches uniform selection’s almost optimal distortion guarantees and additionally achieves constant ex-post distortion, a guarantee concerning the resulting panel. The combination matters because the algorithm supplies both kinds of protection rather than requiring a choice between them.
icml-2024-can-a-few-decide-for-many-the-.tldr: Under a metric preference model, small randomly selected panels can achieve almost optimal decision distortion.

paragraphs: This paper studies centralized assignment when institutions have limited places and candidates have preferences over those institutions. The central selector seeks high total utility while accounting for candidates’ choices. The difficulty is that observed utilities systematically underestimate the true utilities of candidates in some groups, so the scores used for assignment can misrepresent their value.

The authors first show that existing algorithms can perform poorly under this bias. Their selections may sacrifice true utility and create large differences between groups in the fraction of candidates who obtain preferred choices. This connects biased evaluation to both institutional outcomes and the distribution of opportunities that candidates actually want.

The proposed algorithm addresses these two objectives together. Under distributional assumptions, the authors prove that it nearly maximizes true utility while achieving near-optimal group fairness with respect to preferences. They also provide extensive experiments on real and synthetic data, including settings where those assumptions may not hold. These experiments broaden the empirical assessment, while the formal guarantee remains tied to the stated assumptions.
icml-2024-centralized-selection-with-pre.tldr: An assignment algorithm offers conditional guarantees for both true utility and fairness in candidates’ preferred placements despite biased evaluations.

paragraphs: In standard reinforcement learning from human feedback, a language model chooses many tokens before receiving one reward for its entire answer. That leaves training with a sparse signal: many individual decisions share a single final evaluation. This paper asks whether information already computed inside the reward model can make that signal more useful.

The method uses the reward model’s attention weights to distribute the completion’s reward across its tokens. This gives feedback throughout the answer and highlights tokens identified as important by those weights. Because it reuses information produced by the transformer reward model, the approach requires neither an additional model nor extra computational cost, according to the authors.

The authors prove that the redistribution is equivalent to potential-based reward shaping, which preserves the optimal policy. Thus, the training signal changes without changing which policy is optimal under the objective. Experiments show more stable training and faster learning. They also indicate that the method may reach better local optima in practical cases, a qualified benefit distinct from the theoretical preservation result.
icml-2024-dense-reward-for-free-in-reinf.tldr: Reusing reward-model attention produces token-level feedback that preserves the optimal policy and empirically improves RLHF training.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the categories a system is meant to handle. Vision-language models such as CLIP enable this without training on in-distribution data. However, building a text classifier using only the accepted class labels restricts how much of the model’s broader recognition ability can contribute to detecting unfamiliar inputs.

The proposed EOE method uses a large language model to imagine potential outlier categories without accessing actual outlier data. Prompts based on visual similarity produce labels tailored to the detection problem. A new scoring function then incorporates a penalty associated with these potential outliers, helping distinguish difficult unfamiliar samples from accepted ones.

This expands the text descriptions available to the detector beyond its closed set of target classes. The authors evaluate the approach on far, near, and fine-grained out-of-distribution detection, reporting state-of-the-art performance across these tasks. They also demonstrate effective scaling to ImageNet-1K. The stated results support using generated category descriptions as useful detection evidence even when real outlier examples are unavailable.
icml-2024-envisioning-outlier-exposure-b.tldr: EOE uses language-model-generated outlier labels to improve zero-shot detection without accessing actual outlier data.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must pursue reward while satisfying safety constraints. Estimating those constraints can be especially difficult because the signals indicating them are sparse. This paper addresses that learning problem by focusing on how the agent represents its state, rather than treating the raw observations as equally informative about safety.

The proposed Feasibility Consistent Safe Reinforcement Learning framework combines representation learning with objectives aimed at feasibility. Its goal is to extract information relevant to safety from the raw state. Self-supervised learning and a safety metric designed to be easier to learn help improve both constraint estimation and policy learning. The representation is therefore trained to support the safety judgments needed when choosing actions.

The authors evaluate the method on tasks with vector observations and tasks with image observations. Their experiments demonstrate better safety-aware embeddings and stronger performance than previous representation learning baselines. These findings support feasibility-focused representation learning as a way to improve the information available for safe control; the abstract presents empirical improvements rather than an unconditional guarantee that every learned action is safe.
icml-2024-feasibility-consistent-represe.tldr: FCSRL learns representations focused on feasibility to improve safety estimation and policy learning across vector and image tasks.

paragraphs: Investigating training-data bias often requires identifying where a model behaves differently across subgroups. This paper proposes an automated way to find such leads by looking for feature importance disparities. A disparity occurs when a feature has much more or much less influence within a subgroup than it does across the dataset overall.

The method takes a dataset containing protected and unprotected features, observed outcomes, and a regressor that predicts those outcomes. It returns a feature together with a subgroup in which that feature’s influence differs substantially from its overall influence. This gives practitioners a specific relationship to investigate, connecting a model input to a particular part of the training population.

Across four datasets and four common feature importance methods, the authors efficiently identify large disparities even when the candidate subgroup class is exponentially large. In practice, the resulting groups correspond to potentially serious bias issues under standard fairness metrics. The findings support the method as an aid to investigation: a detected disparity points toward a concern, while the appropriate intervention remains dependent on context.
icml-2024-feature-importance-disparities.tldr: Searching for subgroup differences in feature importance can efficiently identify promising leads for investigating data bias.

paragraphs: Some statistical methods treat a probability distribution itself as a random object. Comparing such objects requires a distance between laws of random probability measures, adding a level beyond comparing ordinary distributions. This paper examines the Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein distance used for that purpose and identifies a substantial obstacle to estimating it from samples.

The authors prove that the infinite-dimensional space of probability measures severely worsens this distance’s sample complexity. Its convergence is slower than any polynomial rate in sample size. Consequently, the appeal of the distance’s mathematical structure comes with a demanding statistical estimation problem in the setting analyzed.

They introduce hierarchical integral probability metrics as an alternative that retains many desirable properties while achieving a parametric convergence rate. The new distance metrizes weak convergence, meaning that convergence under the distance captures that statistical notion of convergence. It also supports low-complexity numerical estimation from samples and analytical upper and lower bounds. Together, these properties make the proposal useful for both estimating comparisons and reasoning about them mathematically.
icml-2024-hierarchical-integral-probabil.tldr: Hierarchical integral probability metrics compare random probability measures with substantially better sample convergence than Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein.

paragraphs: How much can an attention layer’s output change when its input changes slightly? A Lipschitz constant quantifies this sensitivity, making it relevant to both robustness and expressive power. This paper studies the local Lipschitz properties of self-attention and masked self-attention, examining how sequence length and layer normalization affect them.

For inputs of length n within any compact set, the authors establish an upper bound proportional to the square root of n. They show that this bound is tight for reasonable sequence lengths, so its dependence on length captures attainable sensitivity in that range. The compact-set qualification is part of the result and matters when interpreting its scope.

For sufficiently long sequences, the square-root bound is no longer tight. In this mean-field regime, the paper gives an upper bound and a matching lower bound that do not depend on sequence length. It also develops a new mean-field framework for masked attention. Experiments using pretrained and randomly initialized BERT and GPT-2 support the theoretical account of these different sensitivity regimes.
icml-2024-how-smooth-is-attention-d6d0e5.tldr: Attention’s sensitivity has a tight square-root sequence-length bound in one regime and length-independent bounds in a sufficiently long-sequence regime.

paragraphs: A dynamic network may be observed only through its connections aggregated over time and its changing row and column totals. Reconstructing the network at individual times from these summaries is an inference problem. Iterative proportional fitting, also called Sinkhorn’s algorithm, has shown empirical promise here, but its statistical justification has been unclear.

This paper identifies a generative network model for which iterative proportional fitting recovers maximum likelihood estimates. That supplies a specific setting in which the procedure has a principled estimation interpretation. The model also exposes assumptions implicit in using the algorithm and supports error bounds that depend on the network’s structure.

The authors additionally address a practical difficulty: iterative proportional fitting can fail to converge on sparse network data. They introduce an algorithm that guarantees convergence while making minimal changes to the network structure. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the practical value of the analysis and the proposed repair. Together, the contributions explain when the existing procedure is statistically justified and how to handle a structural obstacle to using it.
icml-2024-inferring-dynamic-networks-fro.tldr: A generative model gives iterative proportional fitting a statistical foundation for dynamic network inference and supports a convergence repair for sparse data.

paragraphs: Custom analog circuit design often involves searching over circuit topologies through many simulation iterations. LaMAGIC explores a different route: supervised finetuning of a language model to generate an optimized circuit design from a custom specification in one pass. The work focuses on topology generation, the problem of specifying the circuit’s connection structure.

A central challenge is representing a circuit graph in a form suitable for an autoregressive language model. The authors develop and analyze several input and output formulations, aiming for canonical representations that work with sequential generation. This makes the representation of the design problem an important part of the method, alongside the language model itself.

The experiments report success rates reaching 96% at a tolerance of 0.01. The authors also test scalability and adaptability on more complex circuits. An adjacency-matrix formulation paired with floating-point inputs is especially effective in their findings, suggesting suitability for more intricate designs. The reported success is an experimental result, and the broader contribution is a framework for studying language models as generators of circuit graphs.
icml-2024-lamagic-language-model-based-t.tldr: LaMAGIC finetunes a language model to generate analog circuit topologies in one pass, reporting success rates up to 96%.

paragraphs: MagicPose addresses the problem of generating new images of a person from a reference image while controlling their pose and facial expression. The intended result preserves the person’s identity as their depicted movement changes. The method uses a diffusion model for this two-dimensional retargeting task, drawing on existing image-generation knowledge.

The authors introduce a two-stage training strategy to separate motion control from appearance. First, they pretrain a block responsible for appearance control. They then learn pose control that is disentangled from appearance. This separation is designed to support changes in movement while retaining control over visual attributes, including the body, face, clothing-related appearance, and even the background.

The paper reports robust appearance control and good generalization to unseen identities and complex poses without additional finetuning. That matters for using a reference image of a new person without separately adapting the model to that individual. MagicPose can also serve as a plug-in or extension to Stable Diffusion, making the proposed control mechanism usable within that image-generation framework.
icml-2024-magicpose-realistic-human-pose.tldr: MagicPose separates appearance and motion control to retarget human poses and expressions while preserving identity from a reference image.

paragraphs: Human feedback can contain different and conflicting preferences, yet conventional RLHF combines that feedback into a single reward model. This paper examines the consequences of that compression. The authors derive an impossibility result for alignment using a single reward, highlighting its insufficiency for representing diverse human preferences in the setting they study.

Their alternative learns a mixture of reward models using expectation-maximization. This allows the preference data to be represented through multiple reward models instead of one shared evaluation. The alignment step then uses a MaxMin objective inspired by the egalitarian principle in social choice: it gives attention to the least well-served preferences represented by the objective.

The authors evaluate the method with GPT-2 and Tulu2-7B and report that it is effective when human preferences are diverse. These experiments connect the representational argument to language-model alignment at different scales. The paper also states that its findings extend to reinforcement learning more generally, where representing several human preferences can likewise matter for defining what an agent should optimize.
icml-2024-maxmin-rlhf-alignment-with-div.tldr: MaxMin-RLHF combines multiple reward models with an egalitarian objective to better account for diverse human preferences.

paragraphs: In some reinforcement learning applications, feedback naturally arrives only after an entire episode. The learner observes the sum of the rewards, without seeing which individual steps contributed which amounts. This paper studies that aggregate bandit feedback setting, where learning must proceed from an overall outcome rather than a sequence of separately observed rewards.

Earlier work addressed this problem in tabular environments with a small assumed number of states. The authors extend it to linear function approximation, allowing the analysis to use a structured representation rather than a separate entry for every state. Within that setting, they develop two efficient algorithms with near-optimal regret guarantees. Regret describes the performance lost while learning relative to the comparison used in the analysis.

One algorithm is value-based and optimistic, using a new randomization technique involving an ensemble of Q-functions. The other directly optimizes the policy through a new hedging scheme over that ensemble. These provide two algorithmic routes to strong learning guarantees despite the absence of individual reward observations.
icml-2024-near-optimal-regret-in-linear-.tldr: Two efficient algorithms achieve near-optimal regret in linear MDPs when only each episode’s total reward is observed.

paragraphs: An optimizer can influence the solutions reached during training beyond what is explicitly specified by the loss. Earlier analyses of gradient descent used ordinary differential equations to approximate its trajectory and found that finite step sizes introduce terms penalizing the gradient’s two-norm. This paper asks how that implicit effect changes for RMSProp and Adam.

The authors prove that analogous regularization effects depend on the optimizer’s hyperparameters and the stage of training. The relevant quantity is also different: the differential-equation terms involve a perturbed one-norm of the loss gradients. Depending on the conditions, these terms can penalize that quantity or impede its reduction, with the latter behavior described as typical.

This means that the regularization interpretation established for gradient descent does not transfer uniformly to these adaptive optimizers. The direction of their implicit influence matters, as well as the quantity being affected. The paper supplements the theory with numerical experiments and discusses possible consequences for generalization, without claiming a universal generalization improvement from the derived effects.
icml-2024-on-the-implicit-bias-of-adam-1.tldr: Adam and RMSProp have implicit gradient effects whose direction depends on hyperparameters and training stage.

paragraphs: A decision maker in an online auction must choose actions repeatedly while controlling costs and meeting return-on-investment requirements. This paper studies the broader online learning problem behind such decisions. Existing adversarial primal-dual approaches require advance knowledge of strict-feasibility parameters and a strictly feasible offline solution at every round, assumptions the authors identify as impractical.

The proposed framework adds weakly adaptive regret minimizers to standard primal-dual methods. Its dual-balancing mechanism keeps dual variables sufficiently small without knowing the Slater parameter that measures strict feasibility. Controlling these variables matters because they govern how constraint considerations enter the learning process alongside the reward objective.

The authors prove no-regret guarantees under both stochastic and adversarial inputs without the two earlier requirements. This combines guarantees for both input regimes while relaxing the feasibility knowledge and round-by-round feasibility assumptions. They also show how to instantiate the framework for optimal bidding in practically relevant mechanisms, including first-price and second-price auctions. The contribution connects a general constrained learning analysis to concrete bidding settings.
icml-2024-online-learning-under-budget-a.tldr: Weakly adaptive learning yields budget- and ROI-constrained no-regret guarantees without two restrictive feasibility assumptions.

paragraphs: This position paper examines whether human-written and machine-generated text can be distinguished as language models improve. Its argument centers on the distributions of the two kinds of text. The authors provide evidence for detection being feasible with sufficient data, except when those distributions are indistinguishable across their entire support.

Using information theory, they derive sample-complexity bounds that relate reliable detection to the amount of text available. That quantity can increase through more samples or longer sequences. As machine text becomes closer to human text, detection becomes harder, but the analysis supports its remaining possible when adequate evidence is available. This is a conditional possibility claim rather than a guarantee for every individual passage.

The empirical study varies sample sizes and sequence lengths across several datasets, text generators, and detection methods. The findings support the theoretical account and align with previously reported observations about the usefulness of longer sequences. The contribution is therefore both an argument about detectability and guidance on the quantity of evidence that reliable detection may require.
icml-2024-position-on-the-possibilities-.tldr: The paper argues that AI-text detection remains possible with enough data when human and machine text distributions are distinguishable.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems combine information from different kinds of inputs to make a joint decision. When those inputs change in an open environment, the combination may also need to change. This paper addresses the reliability of that dynamic fusion process, arguing that many existing methods lack theoretical guarantees and can settle on suboptimal combinations.

The proposed Predictive Dynamic Fusion framework analyzes fusion through generalization: how well learned behavior carries beyond the training data. It derives a predictable quantity called Collaborative Belief using Mono-Confidence and Holo-Confidence. The authors prove that this construction reduces an upper bound on generalization error. That result provides theoretical support for the design, rather than claiming that every prediction’s error must decrease.

The framework additionally uses relative calibration to adjust predicted Collaborative Belief in response to potential uncertainty. This connects the theoretical fusion quantity to the practical problem of imperfect confidence predictions. Experiments on multiple benchmarks report superior performance, providing empirical support alongside the bound. The contribution combines a principled fusion objective with a calibration mechanism for using it.
icml-2024-predictive-dynamic-fusion-879d.tldr: Predictive Dynamic Fusion combines theoretically motivated confidence estimates and calibration to improve multimodal fusion.

paragraphs: Continual self-supervised learning must develop useful representations from new data while preserving what earlier learning established. The proposed Pseudo-Negative Regularization framework addresses this tension using pseudo-negatives produced through model-based augmentation. These supply training signals intended to reduce contradictions between newly learned representations and knowledge captured by an earlier model.

For contrastive methods based on InfoNCE, the framework defines symmetric pseudo-negatives using both current and previous models. It places them in the main learning loss as well as the regularization loss. The design therefore makes the relationship between old and new representations part of both current learning and the mechanism intended to preserve earlier knowledge.

The authors also adapt the idea to non-contrastive methods, which do not ordinarily use negatives. There, a pseudo-negative comes from the previous model’s output for a differently augmented version of the anchor, and enters the regularization term asymmetrically. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art representation learning performance in continual self-supervised settings, supporting the framework’s ability to balance adaptation to new information with stability.
icml-2024-regularizing-with-pseudo-negat.tldr: Pseudo-Negative Regularization uses current and previous models to balance new learning with representation stability.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel in an image. Scribble supervision reduces annotation effort by asking for marks on only some pixels, then using those labels to help classify the rest. The central learning challenge is to extend the sparse supervision across the image while making effective use of the available visual features.

This paper identifies a weakness in existing propagation methods: they often overlook features of pixels that have already been classified. The proposed method uses feature prototypes to augment scribble supervision. These prototypes provide representative feature information that can contribute to the propagation process, incorporating information beyond the original sparse marks.

The approach matters because it targets how limited annotations are used, which is central to the appeal of scribble-based training. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for scribble-supervised semantic segmentation on PASCAL VOC 2012. The stated finding supports prototype-based feature augmentation as an effective way to improve full-image segmentation from sparse labels within that evaluated setting.
icml-2024-scribble-supervised-semantic-s.tldr: Feature prototypes improve the use of sparse scribble annotations, achieving state-of-the-art segmentation results on PASCAL VOC 2012.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from an existing collection of trajectories. This paper shows that adding more trajectories can hurt when they come from related but different tasks. The authors introduce MOOD, a testbed with heterogeneous data sources, and find that existing methods deteriorate considerably as this additional data enters the offline buffer.

To investigate that counterintuitive result, they conduct a large empirical study and test several explanations. Their findings point to targeted scale as a more influential factor than algorithmic considerations in the studied setting. In particular, increasing the size of the policy helps simple methods handle the more diverse data.

The authors show that AWAC and IQL with larger policies overcome the failure modes caused by adding data in MOOD. These versions also notably outperform previous state-of-the-art algorithms on D4RL. The practical implication of the experiments is that policy capacity deserves attention when learning from mixed sources: the benefit of additional data depends partly on the learning system’s ability to use it.
icml-2024-simple-ingredients-for-offline.tldr: Experiments show that larger policies let simple offline RL methods overcome performance losses from adding heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: A language model accessed through an API can conceal its parameters while still revealing information about its internal structure through its outputs. This paper introduces an attack that recovers precise information from production language models using typical API access. Its target is the transformer’s embedding projection layer, recovered up to symmetries.

The authors report extracting the entire projection matrices of OpenAI’s Ada and Babbage models for less than $20. From this, they confirm hidden dimensions of 1024 and 2048, respectively. These results demonstrate recovery of a substantial model component, with the symmetry qualification specifying the sense in which the recovered parameters correspond to the original layer.

For GPT-3.5-turbo, the authors recover the exact hidden dimension and estimate that extracting its whole projection matrix would cost less than $2,000 in queries. That cost is an estimate, distinct from the completed extractions. The paper also discusses potential defenses and mitigations, along with possible future extensions. Its central finding is that black-box access can expose more internal model information than merely observable behavior.
icml-2024-stealing-part-of-a-production-.tldr: Typical API access enabled recovery of production language models’ projection layers up to symmetries and exposed hidden dimensions.

paragraphs: Language models and multimodal models can make decisions across many tasks, but this paper argues that their planning remains centered in language and lacks visual and spatial imagination. The authors propose a framework that performs visual planning and language planning concurrently. It is designed for tasks with different input forms, rather than only tasks that already contain both images and text.

The two planning modes have complementary intended roles. Visual planning captures detailed information about the environment, while language planning supports logical coherence across the overall process. The brain comparison in the title motivates this combination; the substantive proposal is to incorporate both forms of planning into the task-solving framework.

The authors evaluate the approach on vision-language, vision-only, and language-only tasks. They report superior performance, interpreting the results as evidence that combined planning can improve contextually aware execution. Testing all three input categories is relevant to the framework’s intended breadth: its potential value is tied to how it plans, not solely to whether the original task supplies multiple modalities.
icml-2024-using-left-and-right-brains-to.tldr: Concurrent visual and language planning improves reported performance across multimodal, vision-only, and language-only tasks.
